title: Development of nanosized (NiZn) 1−x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /CNT hybrid filler for polymer composites with enhanced microwave absorption capacity
abstract: Abstract The intensive development of radio-electronic technology has resulted in additional electromagnetic (EM) pollution and problems with EM interference, which has led to the creation of EM absorbing materials. This research presents the development of new polymer composites based on a filler that combines the advantages of the electrophysical properties of multi-walled carbon nanotubes (CNTs) with the magnetic tunability of substituted spinel ferrites (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4  ( x  = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1) and a crystalline polychlorotrifluoroethylene matrix, designed for effective absorption of EM microwave radiation. The (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4  /CNT fillers (0 ≤  x  ≤ 1) were synthesised by co-precipitation, and their spinel crystal structure was confirmed by X-ray diffraction and Raman spectroscopy. The magnetic properties of (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /CNT fillers demonstrated typical superparamagnetic characteristics for single-domain nanoparticles, with maximum saturation magnetization values of 74.1 emu/g at  x  = 0.75. The absorption, reflection and transmission coefficients (1–40 GHz) of the fillers and polymer composites based on them, as well as the reflection coefficient on a metal plate, were calculated by the measured complex dielectric permittivity and complex magnetic permeability in the high-frequency range using the waveguide method. It has been shown that the introduction of a filler into a polymer matrix in an amount of 0.0025 to 0.015 volume fractions allows control their absorption properties, as well as shifting the frequency range of the maximum peak values of the absorption coefficient. The highest absorption coefficients, both in free space and on a metal plate, were observed for three-component systems at  x  = 0.5.   Graphical abstract

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The intensive development of radio-electronic technology and the widespread use of satellite transmission, mobile communications and high-speed data transmission (4G, 5G), and wireless communication systems in everyday life have improved people’s quality of life. However, new technologies lead to an increase of electromagnetic radiation levels. Electromagnetic (EM) interference and EM pollution in a wide range of high frequencies are the most important problems of the twenty-first century. EM pollution can not only affect the performance and service life of highly sensitive electronic equipment, but also have an adverse effect on the functioning of biological systems including human health [ 1 ,  2 ]. Therefore, it is important to solve EM interference challenges by developing new high-performance absorbing materials that are lightweight, thin, broadband, have strong absorption properties and are resistant to aggressive environments.

Nowadays, there are many innovative approaches to the development of materials that absorb EM radiation and is important to note that “ single-phase materials ” are being replaced by fundamentally new nanostructured composite materials, in particular those, based on dielectric binders (polymers [ 3 ,  4 ,  5 – 6 ], ceramics [ 7 ,  8 ]) and fillers (conductive and magnetic components) of various structures (carbon nanotubes [ 9 ,  10 ], graphene nanoplatelets [ 11 ,  12 – 13 ], graphene oxide [ 14 ,  15 – 16 ], carbon fibers [ 17 ,  18 ], bimetallic magnetic nanoparticles [ 19 ,  20 ], soft magnetic and glassy metals [ 21 ,  22 – 23 ], ferrites [ 24 ,  25 ]). In addition, functional materials with hierarchical architecture are also attracting attention, as, it is the multi-level organization of the material structure that allows to significantly improve the absorbing properties [ 26 ,  27 ]. Of particular interest, both from a scientific and industrial point of view, are nanostructured composites with controlled absorption and reflection of high-frequency EM waves, in which the filler combines different electrodynamic parameters. One of the advantages of such materials is the ability to easily regulate their parameters by changing the concentration of the filler introduced into the composite, the thickness of the composite and the selection of components with the required electrodynamic properties. In particular, literature review [ 28 ,  29 ,  30 – 31 ] shows, that the synthesis of nanosized fillers based on carbon nanomaterials of various structures, modified with spinel ferrites, and obtaining functional polymer composites based on them effectively interact with EM radiation. It is possible to control/change some electrophysical parameters in carbon nanomaterial/ferrite fillers, namely complex dielectric permittivity and complex magnetic permeability, which determine the microwave absorption properties of the material. The use of different structures of carbon substrates [ 32 ,  33 – 34 ] and ferrite composition at the nanoscale allows the above-mentioned complex quantities to be changed. Substituted ferrites (SFs) are particularly popular as magnetic components in carbon nanomaterial/ferrite fillers because they are characterized by various losses (magnetic loss caused by natural magnetic losses, exchange resonance, and dielectric loss as a result of interphase polarization and relaxation) [ 35 ,  36 ]. It is known that the microstructure and composition of ferrite materials have a significant effect on their properties, including structural, magnetic, optical and electrical characteristics [ 37 ,  38 – 39 ]. The functional properties of ferrites can be regulated by changing the number of bonds of iron ions in a multicomponent oxide system by introduction of substituting ions or creating oxygen deviation from stoichiometry. Furthermore, the controlled shift of the ferrite absorption maximum peak in the microwave range can be regulated by changing the amount of substituting and obtaining a continuous series of SFs with the same substituting ion allows for the expansion of the absorption bandwidth in the high-frequency range.

It is well known that impedance of an absorbing material must be close to the impedance of the surrounding space to achieve minimal reflection on the front surface of the material, as a result of which EM waves can penetrate the material and be converted into thermal energy or dissipated through interference [ 40 ,  41 ].Therefore, maximum penetration of EM waves into the material is an essential requirement for good absorption. Polymer matrices can be a universal tool for solving the problem of tailoring the impedance of the surrounding space and the impedance of the absorbing material, due to the possibility of modifying the necessary properties [ 42 ,  43 ]. By selecting polymer matrices with specific dielectric and magnetic properties, it is possible to create polymer composite materials that allow incident microwaves to penetrate the material, thereby not only increasing EM absorption, but also improving the production capabilities, performance characteristics, and functionality of such materials [ 44 ,  45 ,  46 ,  47 ,  48 – 49 ]. In addition, the microstructural characteristics of polymer composites can influence the EM absorption. In particular, the size, shape, and concentration of carbon nanomaterials/ferrite fillers can change the type of frequency dispersion of dielectric permittivity and magnetic permeability, which has the effect on the frequency position of the absorption peak [ 25 ,  30 ,  50 ]. However, innovative approaches to the synthesis of nanostructured fillers and strategies for designing polymer composites based on them with excellent properties and more versatile application functions need to be further investigated.

Our preliminary studies [ 30 ] of hybrid fillers based on multi-walled carbon nanotubes (CNTs) modified with substituted ferrite (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4  ( x  = 0, 0.5 and 1) have shown an increase in both magnetic permeability and dielectric permittivity at a frequency of 9 GHz, increasing the efficiency of absorption of EM waves as well as a broadening microwave absorption range from 12 to 20 GHz. This study successfully demonstrates that the incorporation of carbon nanotubes decorated with substituted ferrite nanoparticles into an epoxy matrix allows for the regulation of absorbing properties in the microwave region at specific studied filler concentrations.

In this work, polychlorotrifluoroethylene (PCTFE) was proposed as the polymer matrix, which is characterized by exceptional properties: chemical and thermal stability, non-flammability, low degree of chemical and physical degradation, excellent tribological and mechanical properties, resistance to environmental factors and biocompatibility [ 51 ,  52 ]. Multi-walled carbon nanotubes (CNTs) modified with substituted ferrites (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4  of various compositions were used as nanostructured carbon fillers for the microwave absorption. SFs nanoparticles provide controlled magnetic permeability and magnetic loss through ion substitution, while carbon-based structures allow supply for high electrical conductivity, interfacial polarization effects, and structural integration in polymer matrices.

The aim of this study was to synthesize of new, promising nanostructured fillers based on multi-walled carbon nanotubes modified with substituted ferrites (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4  with different compositions ( x  = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1), and to develop polymer-filled systems based on them that interact with microwave electromagnetic radiation.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: In this work, commercially available reagents of analytical grade were used without further purification: iron (III) nitrate nonahydrate Fe(NO 3 ) 3 ·9H 2 O, manganese (II) nitrate hexahydrate Mn(NO 3 ) 2 ·6H 2 O, nickel (II) nitrate hexahydrate Ni(NO 3 ) 2 ·6H 2 O, zinc nitrate hexahydrate Zn(NO 3 ) 2 ·6H 2 O (Chempur Co., Poland). Hydrazine monohydrate with a purity of 98% (64 – 65% of N 2 H 4 ) and multi-walled carbon nanotubes (C ≥ 95%, average length 5 μm, average diameter 6–9 nm) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Polyvinylpyrrolidone (K—90) produced by Carl Roth GmbH Co. with a molar mass of 900,000–1,200,000 g/mol, a density 1,2 g/cm 3 , and a melting point 130 °C was used, as well as polychlorotrifluoroethylene (PCTFE) powder (F-3 M(A) TU 6-05-1812-87).

sections.heading: Synthesis of (NiZn) 1-x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /CNT powders
paragraphs: Carbon nanotubes (0.04 vol. fraction) were modified with substituted spinel ferrites (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4  ( x  = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1) using a co-precipitation method in the presence of hydrazine hydrate as a reducing agent. First, the required amount of CNTs was dispersed in deionized water (DI) using an ultrasonic homogenizer (Bandelin Sonopuls) for 40 min. The stoichiometrically required amounts of Fe(NO 3 ) 3 ·9H 2 O, Ni(NO 3 ) 2 ·6H 2 O, Zn(NO 3 ) 2 ·6H 2 O, and Mn(NO 3 ) 2 ·6H 2 O were dissolved in DI water. An appropriate amount of polyvinylpyrrolidone solution was gradually added to the salt solutions with continuous stirring for 40 min, and then, the mixture was heated to 80 °C. After the mixture has reached 80 °C, an aqueous dispersion of carbon nanotubes was added to the mixture, stirring continuously. Subsequently, an appropriate amount of hydrazine hydrate was added dropwise until the pH of the solution reached to 9.0, and the final mixture was boiled for 4 h. Finally, the powder was separated by magnetic separation, washed with distilled water and dried at 80 °C for 7 h.

sections.heading: Fabrication polymer composites filled with (NiZn) 1−x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /CNT powders
paragraphs: The content of CNTs in all polymer composites (NiZn) 1– x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /CNT–PCTFE ranged from 0.0025 to 0.015 volume fractions ( ϕ ). The required amount of PCTFE powder and synthesized (NiZn) 1−x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /CNT powder was mechanically ground to obtain a homogeneous mixture. The resulting mixture was placed into a press-form and samples were formed at a polymer melting temperature of 232 °C and a pressure of 5 MPa.

sections.heading: Electrophysical measurements
paragraphs: The structure of both pristine substituted ferrites and the ferrites anchored on the surface of CNTs was studied using a Tecnai F20 TWIN transmission electron microscope (TEM) (FEI Company, Hillsboro, Oregon, USA) equipped with an emission gun, operating at an accelerating voltage of 200 kV. Samples were prepared by applying a droplet (6.0  μL) of powdered solution to the grid (Lacey Carbon Film, 200 mesh Copper), and air-dried for 24 h. TEM images were recorded with a Gatan Rio 16 CMOS 4 k camera (Gatan Inc., Pleasanton, California, USA) and processed using Gatan Microscopy Suite (GMS) software (Gatan Inc., Pleasanton, California, USA).

The structural characteristics of the studied samples were also performed by Raman spectroscopy. Raman spectra were recorded on a Witec Alfa M300 + spectrometer with a Nd-YAG laser beam operated with an excitation wavelength of 532 nm and a laser power of 50 mW. Raman spectra were accumulated in 100 scans with an integration time of 3 s, an acquisition range of 0–3800 cm −1 , and a laser power of 1 mW.

The volume magnetic properties of both substituted ferrites and ferrites deposited on carbon nanotube surfaces were investigated using the Vibrating Sample Magnetometer option of the Quantum Design PPMS VersaLab System at room temperature.

The study real (ε′) and imaginary (ε″) components of the complex dielectric permittivity and real (μ′) and imaginary (μ″) components of the complex magnetic permeability of the composites at microwave frequencies (9 GHz) were studied according to the method described in [ 56 ]. Composite samples with a rectangular shape of 10 × 23 mm and a thickness of 2 mm were tested. Electrical conductivity (σ) measurements at low frequencies (100 Hz) were performed using an impedance meter (E7-14) according to the two-contact method [ 57 ] for composite samples with a square shape (10 × 10 mm) and a thickness of 2.5 mm. Graphite electrodes were used for electrical conductivity measurements, and the experimental error did not exceed 5%.

sections.heading: Results and discussion
paragraphs: The crystal structure and phase characteristics of all synthesized samples were determined using X-Ray diffraction analysis. Figure  1  shows X-ray diffraction patterns of as-synthesized pure substituted ferrites (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4  with 0 ≤  x  ≤ 1 in step of 0.25 and their modified derivatives (NiZn) 1- x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.04CNT. The diffractograms show well-defined and intense peaks, confirming high degree of crystallization of the samples without additional peaks caused by unreacted precursors or any impurity. Figure 1 XRD diffraction patterns of as-synthesized samples: (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 a  and (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.04CNT  b .

The main (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4  ferrite phase was characterized by (111), (220), (222), (311), (333), (400), (422), and (440) crystal planes (ICDD card 01-071-4919), which confirmed the formation of a cubic spinel structure for all samples (Fig.  1 a). The diffraction patterns of (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.04CNT nanocomposites also included all the main reflections and planes characteristic of the ferrite phase, indicating the presence of their cubic crystal structure (Fig.  1 b). A slight shift in diffraction peaks (311 plane) was also observed for all synthesized samples in the range 0 <  x  < 1 (Fig.  2 ), indicating distortion of the crystal lattice caused primarily by different ionic radii of the substituted cations (Ni, Zn and Mn). These distortions were manifested as a slight increase in the lattice parameter ( a ,  Å ) in the case of substitution with larger Mn ions in both (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4  ferrites (from 8.407 to 8.433 Å) and (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.04CNT nanocomposites (from 8.412 to 8.432 Å) (Table  1 ). It should be noted that the lattice parameter values obtained for all samples are close to those reported in the literature [ 58 ,  59 ,  60 – 61 ]. A similar tendency of the increasing crystal lattice parameters for Mn 1− x Ni x Fe 2 O 4 , and Mn x Cu 1− x Fe 2 O 4  substituted ferrites has also been published in the literature [ 62 ,  63 ]. Figure 2 Enlarged image of the diffraction peak (311) of nanoparticles: (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 a  and (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.04CNT  b . According to our calculations, the average crystallite sizes of pure SFs and ferrite nanoparticles on the surface of the CNTs ranged from 8.8 to 13.5 nm and from 6.9 to 13.5 nm, respectively. Based on the size of crystallites, it should be noted that as manganese content increases, the crystallites become larger, which may be related to the ionic radii and the growth mechanism. It can also be observed that changes in lattice strain for both pure SFs and (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.04CNT nanocomposites also correlate with changes in the size of their crystallites (Table  1 ). The differences in ionic radii between Ni, Zn and Mn caused variation change in lattice strain for both pure SFs and (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.04CNT nanocomposites. The dislocation density, directly correlated with the change in crystallite size, (Table  1 ) is very high, suggesting large number of Frenkel defects. Considering the tensile nature of lattice strain, it should be noted that substitution with bigger ions leads to the expansion of the unit cell in pure SFs. However, the formation of ferrites on the surface of CNTs causes higher lattice distortion, most likely as a result of surface defects in CNTs that have potential to affect crystal growth.

TEM images of as-synthesized (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4  ferrites with different compositions ( x  = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1) are shown in Fig.  3 . SF samples with complete substitution are characterized by both ultra-fine, single spherical particles (single or multiple rounded shapes) and moderately agglomerated particles. Figure 3 TEM images of synthesized (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4  nanoparticles with  x : 0  a , 0.25  b  0.5  c , 0.75  d  and 1  e .

The SF synthesis method made it possible to obtain nanoparticles with a relatively wide particle size distribution caused by their agglomeration, namely, the minimum and maximum sizes of the nanoparticles were 2 nm and 45 nm, respectively. Statistical analysis of TEM images and histogram fitting using the log–normal function showed the influence of the substitution amount ( x ) on the average size of SF nanoparticles, particularly, with an increase in the Mn ion content in substituted (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4  ferrites, the average size ( d , nm) of nanoparticles increased non-linearly. A smaller average size of nanoparticles ( d  = 8.17 ± 0.5 nm) was found at  x  = 0.25, and a larger one—at  x  = 0.75 ( d  = 13.25 ± 0.5 nm). These results correspond to the size of crystallites obtained in X-ray diffraction analysis (Table  1 ).

TEM images of (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.4CNT nanocomposites (Fig.  4 ) demonstrated the same uniform spherical nanoparticles as those found for substituted ferrites. Carbon nanotubes are also clearly visible in the images. It was also observed that both individual substituted ferrite nanoparticles and clusters of several overlapping nanoparticles are attached to the nanotubes’ walls at various points. Histograms of particle size distribution showed that the size of SF nanoparticles on the surface of CNTs ranged from 2 to 24 nm. Statistical analysis of the histograms revealed the same trend of nonlinear increase in the average size of ferrite nanoparticles on the CNTs surface with increasing Mn ion content in (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4  ferrite as in the case of pure original SFs. The maximum average particle size was  d  = 13.5 ± 0.5 nm at  x  = 0.75, and the minimum value was  d  = 6.88 ± 0.5 nm at  x  = 0, which corresponds to the sizes of ferrite according to the XRD results (Table  1 ). Figure 4 TEM images of synthesized (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.4CNT nanocomposites with  x : 0  a , 0.25  b  0.5  c , 0.75  d  and 1  e .

The detailed structural characteristics of the synthesized samples were investigated using Raman spectroscopy. Figure  5  demonstrates the Raman spectra of as-synthesized pure (NiZn) 1– x Mn x Fe 2 O 4  substituted ferrites with different compositions and (NiZn) 1– x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.04CNT nanocomposites. All samples exhibit typical bands corresponding to three vibrational modes (A 1g , E g  and T 2g ) of spinel structure with the  Fd3m  (O 7 h ) space group. The pure SFs and CNTs modified with SFs with a composition  x  = 0 have Raman bands at 317 (E g ), 494 (T 2g ) and 681 (A 1g ) cm −1 , typical for spinel ferrites substituted with Ni and Zn ions [ 64 ,  65 ]. In the case of increasing Mn ion content in SFs with a composition of 0.25 ≤  x  ≤ 0.75, all samples exhibit characteristic bands for both spinels and have 263 cm −1  and 309 cm −1  (E g ), 471 cm −1  (A 1g ), 216 cm −1  and 645 cm −1  (T 2g ) from MnFe 2 O 4  [ 66 ,  67 ] and 338 cm −1  (E g ), 471 cm −1  (A 1g ), 590 cm −1  and 670 cm −1  (T 2g ) from Ni and Zn substituted ferrite. Samples with a ferrite composition  x  = 1 are characterized by bands typical for MnFe 2 O 4 : 313 cm −1  corresponding to the E g  vibrational mode, 481 cm −1  to the T 2g  vibrational mode and 588 and 639 cm −1  to the A 1g  vibrational mode. The spectra of all (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.04CNT nanocomposites contain typical bands of carbon materials. In particular, the D band, occurring in the region of ~ 1340 cm −1 , results from scattering in the graphite structure, which originates from out of plane vibrations caused by defects containing sp2 carbon. Other characteristic peak for the graphene structure is the G band, appearing in the region of ~ 1580 cm −1 , resulting from in plane vibration of C–C bonds from sp2 orbital, and the third, is the 2D band at 2700 cm −1 , a second-order overtone of a various in plane vibrations [ 68 ,  69 ]. Figure 5 Raman spectra of synthesized samples: (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 ,  a  and (NiZn) 1 −x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.04CNT  b .

The study of changes in magnetic properties accompanying the chemical transformations in of substituted ferrite (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4  with various compositions 0 ≤  x  ≤ 1 were performed based on measurements of magnetization (M) as a function of applied field (H) at room temperature (Fig.  6 ). The saturation magnetization (Ms) was estimated at the maximum field applied, i.e., 3 kOe. Ms for pure SFs increased continuously with increasing Mn content in the examined range (0 ≤  x  ≤ 1), reaching a maximum value of Ms = 77.4 emu/g for  x  = 0.75 (Fig.  6 a, curve  4 ). Conversely, for  x  = 1, Ms exhibited a substantial decrease, reaching a value of 51.3 emu/g (Fig.  6 a, curve  5 ). Magnetization in spinel ferrites with ion substitutions depends on the nature of the introduced ions (magnetic or non-magnetic), their super exchange interactions and their preferences for crystallographic position (sub-lattices A or B, according to Néel’s theory), as well as on the amount of ions introduced. This effect has been widely documented in the literature [ 70 ,  71 ]. A more complex nature of saturation magnetization growth was observed for (NiZn) 1 −x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.04CNT nanocomposites, with the highest Ms value of 74.1 emu/g at  x  = 0.75 (Fig.  6 b, curve  4 ). In addition, a correlation was also established between the crystallite size values and the saturation magnetization of all synthesized samples (Fig.  7 ), which is likely due to the surface effect. In general, the saturation magnetization of magnetic nanoparticles is lower than that of bulk material, because a decrease in crystallite size leads to high surface energy, causing breaking disturbance in the magnetic order in the surface layer of the particles, which reduces the total magnetization [ 72 ,  73 – 74 ]. A similar effect of the nanoscale size of magnetic nanoparticles has been observed previously for different types of ferrites [ 75 ,  76 ]. Based on the results in [ 76 ], the magnetic behaviour of Fe 3 O 4  nanocrystals showed an increase in saturation magnetization values from 25 to 43, 80, and 102 emu/(g Fe) with an increase in nanocrystal size from 4 to 6, 9, and 12 nm, respectively. Figure 6 Magnetization curves of synthesized samples: (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 ,  a  and (NiZn) 1−x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.04CNT  b  with  x : 0 ( 1 ), 0.25 ( 2 ) 0.5 ( 3 ), 0.75 ( 4 ) and 1 ( 5 ). Figure 7 Dependence of saturation magnetization (1) and crystallite size (2) on the substituted content in synthesized samples (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 a  and (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.04CNT  b .

The magnetization hysteresis loops of all synthesized samples (Fig.  6 ) show typical superparamagnetic characteristics for single-domain nanoparticles. Superparamagnetic nanoparticles respond quickly to changes in the magnetic field without residual magnetization and without coercivity. It is well known that the superparamagnetic state depends to a large extent on the particle size, i.e. the smaller the particle size, the stronger the superparamagnetic properties [ 77 ]. The process of reversing the magnetization of a ferrimagnetic particle with a domain structure, i.e. a multi-domain particle, occurs mainly through the displacement of domain boundaries. In this case, the coercivity values are low and increase as the particle size decreases. When the particles become single-domain, the coercivity value reaches its maximum, which is associated with a change in the magnetization reversal mechanism. With a further decrease in particle size below the critical value, there is a decrease in coercivity and residual magnetization, as well as a transition of the nanoparticle to a single-domain superparamagnetic state. In the superparamagnetic state, both the residual magnetization and coercivity are zero [ 72 ]. As reported in the literature [ 67 ,  77 ,  78 ,  79 – 80 ], spinel ferrites exhibit a transition between multi-domain and single-domain magnetic behaviour in nanoparticles of different sizes, depending on the synthesis method. In particular, for nickel ferrite, this size was approximately 53.3 nm (co-precipitation method) [ 81 ], 15 nm (auto-combustion method) [ 82 ], and for CoFe 2 O 4  ferrite it was 6.5 nm (sol–gel auto-combustion method) [ 83 ], 7 nm (co-precipitation method) [ 84 ] and 40 nm (seed-mediated co-precipitation method) [ 85 ].

Figure  8  shows the experimental results of measurements of complex dielectric permittivity ( ε′ , ε″) at a frequency of 9 GHz and conductivity (σ) at a low frequency (100 Hz) for (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.04CNT (0 ≤  x  ≤ 1) systems with PCTFE. With an increase in the volume content 0.0025 ≤  ϕ  ≤ 0.015 of the filler in the polymer matrix, an increase in the values of the investigated parameters  ε′ , ε″ and σ was observed. It is well known that in the microwave frequency range, dielectric properties are most likely caused by interfacial polarization in multicomponent heterogeneous media [ 86 ]. Interfacial polarization occurs as a result of charge accumulation at the conductor/dielectric interfaces, which complicates the relaxation processes. With an increase in the filler concentration in polymer composites, the interfacial specific surface area also increases, which determines the contribution of interfacial polarization and, as a result, an increase in the value of  ε′ . Figure 8 Dependences of the  ε′ a  and ε″  b  at 9 GHz and the electrical conductivity logarithms (σ) at 100 Hz  c  on CNTs volume fractions ( ϕ ) in polymer composite systems (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.04CNT–PCTFE:  x  = 0 ( 1 ) ,  0.25 ( 2 ), 0.5 ( 3 ), 0.75 ( 4 )  and  1 ( 5 ).

In polymer composites, an increase in the volume concentration of carbon nanotubes is typically accompanied by an increase in the ε″ values, which is associated with the formation of conductive paths which, leading to an increase in conduction losses. Consequently, the increase in dielectric losses is mainly due to an increase in polarization and conduction losses. According to our study, the increase in the values of ε′, ε″ and σ in ternary systems with increasing volume content of carbon nanotubes was non-linear, which is due to the presence of the percolation transition (approximately 0.009–0.011 vol. fractions) and corresponds to its threshold value. The maximum values of ε′ and ε″ reached 17.9 and 12.6, respectively, for the (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.04CNT–PCTFE composites ( x  = 1) (Fig.  8 a, b). In the publication [ 87 ], an increase in the values ε′ and ε″ with increasing Mn content was also observed for the superparamagnetic ferrite based on Mn co-doped with Co and Cu, which indicated good dielectric losses.

In EMI shielding theory, when an EM wave is incident on a shielding material, the incident power is divided into reflected, absorbed and transmitted power and the corresponding power coefficients of absorbance ( A ), reflectance ( R ), and transmittance ( T ) are such that  A  +  R  +  T  =  1  [ 89 ,  90 ] .  We can use this relationship to calculate  A  from the results of  R  and  T.

Figure  9  illustrates the frequency dependencies of the calculated absorption ( A ), reflection ( R ), and transmission ( T ) coefficients of substituted ferrites (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4  (a) and (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.04CNT nanocomposites (b) at different manganese ion contents and sample thickness of 2.5 mm. An increase in the absorption coefficient was observed with increasing frequency, reaching maximum values at  x  = 0 for all pure SFs, while the level of transmitted radiation decreased. At the same time, the minimum reflection coefficient slightly shifted towards a higher frequency range with incзreasing manganese ion content in SFs. The EM absorption processes by (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.04CNT nanocomposites exhibit some peculiarities (Fig.  9 b), in particular, at frequencies up to 15 GHz with a certain ion substitution content it occurs more efficiently than in the case of pure ferrite. Composites with  x  = 0.25 and  x  = 0.75 showed the highest values of the absorption coefficient observed up to 20 GHz, and were approximately 1.5 times higher than for samples with  x  = 0 and  x  = 0.5. Figure 9 Frequency dependences of EM wave absorption ( A ), reflection ( R ) and transmission ( T ) coefficients of (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4  substituted ferrites  a  and (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.04CNT nanocomposites  b  with  x : 0 ( 1 ); 0.25 ( 2 ); 0.5 ( 3 ); 0.75 ( 4 ) and 1 ( 5 ).

The increase in the frequency range of the absorption coefficient up to about 20 GHz is probably caused by both the size of the ferrite crystallites and the high saturation magnetization of these samples (Fig.  7 ), and, consequently by higher magnetic losses. Furthermore, for samples with substituted ion contents of  x  = 0 and  x  = 0.5, a decrease in the reflection coefficient was observed near 27 GHz, most likely as a result of improved impedance matching characteristics. These samples also exhibited an identical decrease in the transmission coefficient at frequencies above 20 GHz, indicating enhanced interaction with EM waves. The absorption mechanism of microwave EM radiation for SF-modified carbon nanotube-based is determined by the matching impedance and the ratio of dielectric and magnetic losses.

The polymer matrices that allow EM waves to pass through are able to reduce microwave reflection by acting as an impedance matching layer between free space and the absorbing material, allowing more microwave energy to be transmitted into the material for absorption [ 91 ]. In our case, PCTFE is a polymer matrix that transmits EM waves and provides impedance matching between the (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.04CNT nanocomposites and free space. Figure  10  shows the calculated curves of absorption ( A ), reflection ( R ) and transmission ( T ) coefficients as a function of frequency for polymer composites based on PCTFE and carbon nanotubes modified with substituted ferrites with different manganese ion contents. The thickness of the samples was 2.5 mm. All samples were characterized by an increase in the absorption coefficient to peak values with an increase in the volume content of the filler (0.0025 ≤  ϕ  ≤ 0.015), while the transmission coefficient decreased. With an increase in filler content, a shift of the peak values of the absorption coefficient towards the low frequency range was also observed. In particular, at  x  = 0, there is a shift from 37.5 to 19 GHz; at  x  = 0.25, there is a shift from 30 to 20 GHz; at  x  = 0.5, there is a shift from 36.5 to 17.2 GHz; at  x  = 0.75, there is a shift from 36.5 to 18 GHz and at  x  = 1, there is a shift from 34 to 14.8 GHz. Furthermore, the maximum peak values of the A coefficient for all filler concentrations were observed for polymer composites with a doping amount of manganese ions of  x  = 0.5. Figure 10 Frequency dependences of EM wave absorption ( A ), reflection ( R ) and transmission ( T ) coefficients of polymer based systems (NiZn) 1−x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.04CNT–PCTFE with x: 0  a ; 0.25  b ; 0.5  c ; 0.75  d  and 1  e . Volume fractions of CNTs:  1 —0.0025;  2 —0.005;  3 —0.0075;  4 —0.01;  5 —0.015.

Increasing the concentration of carbon nanotubes (with a high aspect ratio) in polymer systems is reported to create an effective conductive network, which significantly improves electrical properties, in particular by increasing dielectric losses associated with eddy currents and conductance loss. However, the mismatch between the impedance of air and highly conductive material causes waves to reflect at the boundary, resulting in a significant portion of the EM wave energy being reflected and only a small portion being transmitted to the absorbing material. In our study, polymer composites containing the maximum filler concentration ( ϕ  ≥ 0.015), corresponding to high conductivity, have the highest reflection coefficients and the lowest transmission coefficients.

Figure  11  illustrates the frequency dependencies of the calculated  R met  parameters [ 94 ,  95 ] for the polymer system (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.04CNT–PCTFE at different Mn ion contents and the thickness of the samples is 2.5 mm. For all polymer composites, low  R met  values were observed in the 12–14 GHz frequency range, except for composites with the lowest filler content ( ϕ  ≤ 0.0025). In particular, the reflection coefficient  R met  is 0–10% (less than -20 dB) for polymer composites with filler content of 0.005 ≤  ϕ  ≤ 0.01 with various SF compositions 0 ≤  x  ≤ 1 in the frequency range of 12–14 GHz. However, it should be noted that samples with  x  = 0.5 (Fig.  11 c) at filler concentrations of 0.0025 and 0.01 reflected less than 10% of EM waves in the frequency ranges of 12–21 GHz and 12–18 GHz, respectively, due to the optimal ratio of complex dielectric permittivity, complex magnetic permeability and sample thickness. Figure 11 Frequency dependences of EM wave reflection coefficients on the metal plate of polymer based systems (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.04CNT–PCTFE with  x : 0  a ; 0,25  b ; 0.5  c ; 0.75  d  and 1  e . Volume fractions of CNTs:  1 —0.0025;  2 —0.005;  3 —0.0075;  4 —0.01;  5 —0.015.

When these terms are achieved, the angular phase difference between the electromagnetic waves reflected from the sample surface and reflected from the metal surface is π/2, reducing the amount of reflected energy.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: Substituted ferrites (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4  with  x  = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, and 1, as well as their modified derivatives (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /CNT with a carbon nanotube concentration of 0.04 volume fractions were synthesized by co-precipitation in the presence of a reducing agent (hydrazine hydrate). The results of X-ray diffraction and Raman spectroscopy confirmed the formation of a single-phase cubic spinel structure (space group  Fd3m ) for all samples in the Mn ion substitution range 0 ≤  x  ≤ 1. Based on X-ray diffraction, it was established that the average sizes of pure SF and ferrite crystallites on the surface of carbon nanotubes were 8.8–13.5 nm and 6.9–13.5 nm, respectively, depending on the Mn ion substitution values, which corresponds to the average sizes of SF nanoparticles according to the results of transmission electron microscopy.

Magnetic measurements performed using VSM at room temperature revealed that both pure SF nanoparticles and SF nanoparticles on the surface of CNTs demonstrated typical superparamagnetic characteristics for single-domain nanoparticles. With increasing Mn content in both pure SF nanoparticles and (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /CNT nanocomposites, symbatic behaviour of ferrite nanoparticle crystallite size and saturation magnetization was also observed, caused by surface effects. The maximum saturation magnetization values for pure SFs and synthesized SF/carbon nanotube nanostructures were 77.4 emu/g and 74.1 emu/g, respectively, with a substitution content of  x  = 0.75.

Polymer composites based on a crystalline polychlorotrifluoroethylene matrix with synthesized (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /CNT nanostructures (0 ≤  x  ≤ 1) were developed. In three-component systems, an increase in ε′, ε″ (9 GHz) and σ (100 Hz) values was observed with increasing filler concentration, reaching maximum values at an ionic substitution content  x  = 1.

The experimental values of complex dielectric permittivity and complex magnetic permeability obtained for synthesized pure SFs and (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /CNT nanostructures, as well as polymer composites based on them, were used to calculate the absorption, reflection, and transmission coefficients in the frequency range of 1–40 GHz. The processes of EM wave absorption by (NiZn) 1− x Mn x Fe 2 O 4 /0.04CNT nanocomposites in the frequency range from 1 to 20 GHz are more efficient with manganese ion substitution contents  x  = 0.25 and  x  = 0.75 compared to unmodified SFs due to better impedance matching. Polymer nanocomposites were characterized by an increase in the absorption coefficient to peak values and their shift to lower frequencies with an increase in filler concentration for all substitution contents. The highest absorption coefficients were observed for three-component systems at  x  = 0.5. High absorption parameters were observed for polymer composites (filler content 0.005 ≤  ϕ  ≤ 0.01) on a metal plate in the frequency range of 12–14 GHz and were caused by impedance and thickness matching. Particularly, polymer composites doped with manganese ion substitution content x = 0.5 were characterized by the lowest reflection (0–10%) in the wider frequency range of 12–21 GHz and 12–18 GHz at  ϕ  = 0.0025 and  ϕ  = 0.01, respectively.

This study clearly demonstrated that the design of nanostructured composite materials based on carbon nanotubes modified with substituted ferrites allows for the tailoring of absorption properties in the microwave range at optimal proportions of filler concentration and substitution content in SFs. Absorbing material coatings on metal surfaces can significantly reduce energy of EM wave reflections.
